Representatives of member states, Afghan political and civil society figures, experts, colleagues, and friends of Afghanistan, as well as those who are watching this event live. Five years have passed since the Taliban's military and forced return to power in Afghanistan. During these five years, much of the international response has understandably focused on managing immediate crises, humanitarian needs, economic deterioration, terrorism, refugees, narcotics, human rights, and most urgently, the systematic restrictions imposed on women and girls. These issues remain extremely serious. Only last week, the United Nations told the Security Council that there has been no progress on issues of profound concern, including severe restrictions on women and girls, exclusionary governance, the human rights situation, and the continued presence of terrorist groups threatening Afghanistan, the region, and international peace and security. But after five years, I believe we must also ask a broader political question. Where is Afghanistan heading and what is the political end state that Afghans and the international community are actually working toward? Humanitarian assistance is indispensable, but humanitarian assistance cannot resolve a crisis of political legitimacy Even humanitarian aid has declined. Counterterrorism is an immediate security concern but it requires for a responsible and legitimate government committed to its national and international obligations. Economic initiatives require funding and development aid which has been suspended. And engagement, however necessary, cannot become an end in itself. The question should therefore not simply be whether the international community should engage or isolate Afghanistan. The more important question is engagement toward what objective? The objective should be a durable political solution that enable legitimate, inclusive, representative, and accountable governance reflecting the will and aspirations of the Afghan people. And such a solution cannot be designed exclusively outside Afghanistan and then presented to Afghans. It must be Afghan-led and Afghan-owned. That means Afghans must have the central role in defining their political future. It means bringing credible Afghan stakeholders into a genuine political process, including women, youth, civil society, democratic forces, political figures, and other representatives of Afghanistan's diverse society. They must participate where political decisions are actually made. At the same time, an Afghan-led process does not mean Afghanistan can solve these challenges in isolation. Afghanistan's stability is deeply connected to the stability of the region. Terrorism and violent extremism, narcotics trafficking, refugee movements, economic connectivity, water-related challenges, and cross-border tensions do not stop at Afghanistan's borders. This is precisely why Afghanistan's political future is not only an Afghan concern. It has direct implications for regional and international peace and security. Our neighbors, therefore, have an important role. Regional organizations have an important role. Member states have an important role. And the United Nations has an essential role, but there is an important question. The role of international and regional actors should be to facilitate, support, and enable an Afghan-led political process, not to direct it, substitute for it, or determine Afghanistan's political future on behalf of its people. The United Nation has already articulated an ambition for Afghanistan to be at peace with itself and its neighbors, reintegrated into the international community, and meeting its international obligations. Recent UN briefings have also stressed that engagement should not be equated with endorsement of the existing political order. Thank you so much, Madeleine, for giving us the opportunity. And then I would like to take the opportunity to thank the Diana Foundation and also our permanent mission here in New York and all colleagues that are here for being with us. I think the Taliban will return to the table only when isolation become unsustainable. They today believe that they can govern without accountability or legitimacy. That belief must be dismantled through coordinated international pressure and a unified diplomatic front that makes three truths undeniable. One, no regime can survive by erasing half of their populations. Number two, no ideology can silence 40 million people forever. Number three, No government can claim legitimacy without transparency and oversights. So these are the things that maybe if there is pressure, there is no real pressure by the international community. As Ambassador Seikel also mentioned about the sanction and also about political will, unfortunately, there is no political will. If you see the Security Council here, there is no clear vision that what's their vision towards Afghanistan. from the neighbors, from the region, from OIC, from every country, that there is no clear vision. What we can see as Afghan, and especially Afghan women, that all pressure is on the Afghan side. There is no pressure by any countries on the Taliban. The real pressure is on Afghan people. And your second question about the Afghan-led process, an Afghan-led process began when Afghan stops waiting for permission to shape their future. Civil society, as my brother mentioned about the role of civil society, civil society, diaspora networks, religious scholars, youth, and women group can build political momentum outside the Taliban shadow. by defining a national vision rooted in dignity, rights, and justice, developing a credible roadmap for political transition that the international community can support. Number three, create a unified platform where diverse Afghan voices speak with one strategic message. This will be not a parallel government, it's a parallel legitimacy built from the ground up, where Afghans articulate a clear, inclusive alternatives, and Taliban refusal to engage become their weakness, not our weaknesses. Thank you.

Thank you so much. And To build on the the regional discussion that we're having you spent a great deal of time engaging with the OIC you were Afghanistan's first woman elected as a member of the OIC independent human rights Commission Commission So I'd be curious from your perspective, you know, what role you see for the Gulf and the OIC in in Afghanistan and when it comes to issues around the political track what role you see for.

If I start with the Gulf, I think the Gulf holds a unique moral and strategic influence, and it can champion an Islamic narrative that women's rights and education convene credible regional diplomacy and sustain humanitarian and educational lifetime for Afghan girls and Afghan people in general. At the beginning, if you see in the past five years, OIC, immediately after the country has been collapsed, the Secretary General appointed a special Sr. for Afghanistan, Ambassador Tarek, who is a dedicated diplomat, and he is engaged with the Taliban de facto authorities, and a number of statements also came out by different groups of OIC, a number of scholar visitors went to Afghanistan, and then religious groups also. But that's not enough, because unfortunately, as Ambassador Saikal mentioned, that Afghan, and especially Afghan or not at the center of those negotiations. OIC can play a great role, though OIC is not an executive role, but OIC member states, those that they are very much involved in Afghanistan, especially Turkey, Qatar, Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and other strong OIC members, that they can play a great role by interfering to all of these. What OIC can do? OIC is very much involved in the humanitarian assistance also. They have a small office. But what is the gap in the past five years that there is no real monitoring mechanism by OIC member states, that they should play a great role by doing all this. A number of edicts are coming daily, but OIC is silent about that. And also, OIC can maybe do, with help of women's leaders, can become with a action plan on women's rights in Afghanistan, a significant action plan to play a great role. But unfortunately, that's like an OIC member state. So I would like to take the opportunity once again, call on OIC member states, especially now we have a new secretary general dedicated Secretary General that he was a diplomat that play a significant role in Afghan because Taliban are not forever in Afghanistan. Taliban will go. But what we are doing and then what the history will judge, we are looking forward to them Afghanistan nation is the nation that we will become the future of Afghanistan, and the history will judge what role the regional countries and also what role the Islamic countries, especially, build on us, supported us. Taking the opportunity also, I would like to mention about the role of the neighbors, that they are very much important. As I mentioned before, that governments, especially Pakistan, Iran, India, that they are not putting any pressure on Taliban. What they are putting pressure on Afghan generation. And I would like to ask them that do not support madrassas anymore for Afghanistan, because now they are putting bomb on Afghanistan and Afghan civilian, on Afghan people under the name of the terrorism. Thank you so much. Thank you so much. It is a great honor to be here alongside distinguished colleagues. And I would like to express my appreciation to Permanent Mission of Afghanistan, Independent Diplomats, and Indiana Foundation for hosting and organizing this wonderful event. First of all, I would appreciate it if you allow me a little more time for respond to this question and for other questions, I promise I would be brief. Do you allow me? Okay, thank you. Actually, we are facing three critical challenges in this situation. First, a profound crisis of trust. Second, the accelerating loss of Afghanistan's intellectual and professional capital, and third, the effective closure of formal diplomatic channels, making conventional track one engagement limited as a path forward. In this environment of profound distrust, One constituency has maintained across all community, all ethnic group and all political tendency, the trust and respect of Afghan people, its academics and professionals, including professors, journalists, economists, psychologists, IT specialists and so on. But there is a painful paradox here. Afghanistan has lost approximately half of its university faculty since 2021 and 58% of its judges and prosecutors. And unfortunately, most of many of them who left Afghanistan and currently are working in outside of Afghanistan they are working in jobs entirely unrelated to their expertise because their credential has not or are not recognized and no structure channel exists through which their expertise can be directed to their country. As a professor of political science, I think we need to redefine the political participation and inclusive governance, because they have been understood quite differently in Afghan context. and most of practitioners and civil society activists understand them as power sharing, while the meaning goes beyond that. And it includes economic, social, civic, and cultural domination. In light of this, I think the role of professionals and experts and academics is significant. As you know, currently, all formal diplomatic channels are blocked, and, you know, my engagement has not produced a meaningful shift in the Taliban's approach to its international obligations. And I think track two diplomacy is a productive alternative. in this situation, and we can think about that and focus on that. And Afghan academics and professionals are the natural and main actors for track two diplomacy. because all communities trust them and they connected to colleagues inside of Afghanistan. They have knowledge and they are familiar with the context and know what kind of methods is more actionable or you can apply the project or policies or programs. And they can play a significant role in bringing Afghan closer to one another in this situation. And about how can they participate and engage, I can say at least in three areas they can play a significant role. First, in the Doha process working groups, as you know, for this time they have two working groups, including counter narcotics and the private sectors. In this working group and the future working group in Doha process, Afghan economists, psychologists, and legal scholars should be part of the expert layer. providing independent analysts alongside international bodies and other side who are included in the process. Second, in all UN agencies who are working in Afghanistan, who are active in Afghanistan, including UNDP, UNESCO, UNICEF, WHO, and other agencies who are active in Afghanistan and working on Afghanistan, Afghan technical specialists should be engaged in any program design, assessment, monitoring, and in decision-making level because they are familiar with the context and they know what are the real demands of Afghan people. And third, Afghan legal professionals and public policy experts are essential contributors to the independent investigative mechanism. And I think there are many other areas that the professionals can contribute as technical experts, but we can discuss later.

Thank you. Thank you, Zakia. I will I'm going to open the floor for questions because I'd really like us to have an interactive discussion and I'm sure there will be lots of follow-ups around the role of the diaspora and you know, how to bridge the Afghans inside and outside. But maybe before I do that, we've heard a bit about, you know, the role of the region. We've heard about the importance of an Afghan-led and owned process. but a little bit less about specifically what you would like to see from the UN. And so I just be curious before we open up to the floor or ambassador cycle, if you could reflect on what you see as the role of the UN, UNAMA, the new SRSG within this process?

It's been 81 years when the UN was established to prevent trouble, to prevent wars. If you look at the number of wars in the past 81 years, it is quite a number, a large number of wars that we have seen. And we must have lost more than, what, 20 million who lost their lives in the Second World War? Or I don't know how many millions. I just correct me if I'm wrong, but in the case of Afghanistan, it looks like the UNAMA mandate is very reactive, has remained reactive. We see the deterioration, rapid deterioration of human rights while the actual mandate, it says that you should prevent, but UNAMA continues to report on what happens. I understand a review is and hopefully will take place. I think it's important that UNAMA becomes proactive and preventative. That's the expectation of the people of Afghanistan, what we heard, the people who are calling AMU, they all want to be heard. The highest place that they look at is the UN Security Council. And the Council is in a position to really have a fair review of the UNAMA mandate. Not that they bring anything -- well, hopefully they could bring new elements, but taking the existing contents of the mandate serious, because over there, for example, it talks about political outreach. Now, how many times you have seen UNAMA's representative in the conferences of the opposition? Almost none. And the question is why? The mandate says that you should have outreach, equal outreach, and good offices. But it looks like UNAMA has been heavily engaged with the Taliban. And because the Taliban keep warning that if you engage with the opposition, then I will not talk to you. And the same thing goes to the entire Doha process. You go and bring the women around the negotiating table, then we will stay in Kabul. And then you have to say to the Taliban, okay, no, no, no, we will not bring in the women, please come. My fear is that the Doha process at the end of the day may win the Taliban, but they will lose the people of Afghanistan. And remember, the UN, while we have got the GA debate in here, is supposed to be relevant to those who need it most. And at the moment, the people of Afghanistan need the UN most. So do you want to listen to the people of Afghanistan or to those who have taken them hostage? Somewhere you have to understand the diplomatic sensitivities, but I think going too far in the hope of winning the Taliban, in the hope of seeing the Taliban opening girls' schools, and in my mind it will be too late because the curriculum has already been changed. My fear is we might see our young girls turning into terrorists, highly radicalized. So you may see that, but the people of Afghanistan will be completely confused about the UN role and the charter of the UN. So there are other things too. For example, the sanctions regime, which has been there for years, hasn't been reviewed. Still, if you have a look at the sanctions regime, the Taliban or the insurgents of the Republic Anyway, I asked a member of the just this morning, I asked a member of the Council, the Security Council, has the mandate has the sanctions regime been reviewed? No. Is there any plan to review it? No. If anything, there are a couple of members of the Security Council who are just saying that everything is fine in Afghanistan. I shouldn't say a couple, at least one. Everything is fine. So I think we need to really get serious and it looks like it is important for the five permanent members not to see towards Afghanistan through their geopolitical games but through the genuine interest of the 45 million people of Afghanistan. And that's what the charter says. The charter has mandated members of the Security Council to take care of the troubles of the world based on the wishes of their own people, not based on your geopolitical calculations.
Okay, great. Well, then I will hand it back to the ambassador to open up for questions.

Thank you. Thank you so much, Molin, for ably moderating the panel. And now we will open the floor for Q&A and questions. So we have one friend on the right side, please.

Assalamu alaikum and hi, everyone. My name is Fazal Montaz. I'm the chief operating officer for Sahara Programs. And so I have two questions. One is kind of-- my first question is to Asilajon Wardak. Like I don't know, like most of us, what was in this agreement, what it includes, why it's ambiguous, number one. My second question is from Najif Izadhasib. Nargis Nahon from Faragid. I don't have any question, but I have three suggestions. Thank you, Nergis Can, for your suggestions. Any other questions, or we move to the answers first? Yes, please.

Sorry, thank you very much. I'm from the Republic of Liberia. And as we all know, Liberia is a member of the Security Council. But then we end on a note that the Security Council was both culpable for most of the things that are now happening, I mean, in a certain sense, and also had a key to unlocking the current stalemate. I don't, I'm not from Afghanistan, but I have experience personally and our mission tries to say this whenever we have a chance to intervene, that we know what it feels like for a country to be in this state. You are not at war, but you are also not having the fullness of peace. And there are a lot of friendly countries on the Security Council, but every time we get a criticism that the Council isn't thinking much about the situation in Afghanistan. And I think that is a little bit unfair. We know from the perspective of Afghans, there is nothing that can be done to contain the frustration with the current situation. But there are conversations being held on the issue of Afghanistan. The resolution 2626, which was passed before we got on the Council, is different from the current resolution that renewed the mandate of UNAMA 22. So changes are happening in the mandate as part of the process of searching for the leverage point to put pressure on the Taliban. But we all know the Security Council is a consensus-based group. No matter what you want, what you think, you have to form consensus in order for action to be taken. So it is not so hopeless. We think progress is happening. In resolution 2721, the entire roadmap that was outlined in the assessment report on Afghanistan, it was endorsed by the Security Council. And most of the The points in there which were supposed to be reciprocated by the Taliban have been enforced from the perspective of the Security Council, with the exception of one important one, which is the appointment of a special envoy. And that was a sticking point in the last negotiation before the renewal of the UNAMA mandate. It took a long time. I think we even had to do short-term technical go-over in order to extend the negotiation. Over the past four, five weeks, we have had a series of discussions on Afghanistan. That's how important it is. Liberia is an African country representing the A30. Afghanistan is a far on the A30 mechanism. That's how important it is. So I think the problem here is the Security Council knows what it wants for Afghanistan, and that includes the participation of the Afghans in that process. The problem we see from where we sit on the council is the approach, how to get there. What kind of engagement do we want? What's the realistic definition of the mosaic process? If we can find consensus on that, there will be progress in Afghanistan. We had a situation where there was still made in Liberia for a long time. Should the international community deal with the rebel leader Charles Taylor? or just neglecting, even though he had 85% of the country. And that was a big issue. We found a way with the help of the international community to get past that. So I think if we define what kind of engagement the international community should do, because there are some members of the council who feel neglecting the Afghan people because you don't want to deal with the Taliban. will be increasing the humanitarian situation there. While others think engaging with them too much is indirectly legitimizing their control over the country. So we need to really find the friendly voices and push a uniform position instead of recounting the problem and generally criticizing all members of the Council.

How UNAMA can help with this, everything that's going on in Afghanistan. Hi, my name is Meima Murtaza. It's a pleasure to be here. My grandfather was the former ambassador of the UN for 30 years, Dr. Abdul Hakim Tabibi. Hi, my name is Survi Kumar. I'm from the UN Counterterrorism Committee Executive Directorate.
